analysis.one_liner: Federal-state partnerships to cover students' unmet college costs so they can attend in-state public colleges without debt.
analysis.headline: Sponsored by 9 Senate Democrats, the bill was referred to the Senate education committee and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create federal grants to states, matched to what each state already spends on public higher education, on the condition that the state cover every eligible student's unmet cost of attendance at in-state public colleges, cap tuition at 2021 levels (with inflation adjustments), and maintain its own funding. It would also fund historically Black colleges, tribal colleges, and other minority-serving institutions to cover their students' unmet need, and it would make Dreamer students brought to the US as children eligible for federal financial aid. It authorized $84 billion for the first year and $3 billion for minority-serving institutions.
analysis.who_benefits: Students at in-state public colleges — especially Pell Grant recipients and other low-income students, whose unmet cost of attendance would be covered first — plus students at historically Black colleges, tribal colleges, and other minority-serving institutions, and Dreamer students who would become eligible for federal aid for the first time.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Public college students, especially low-income and Pell recipients

how_it_helps.text: States receiving grants must cover each eligible student's unmet financial need — the gap between cost of attendance and expected family contribution plus grant aid — at in-state public colleges, with Pell Grant recipients covered first [S2][S3].

Participating states must cap tuition and fees at public colleges at their level when the law passed, allowing only inflation-based increases, and commit to reducing tuition as state funding rises [S3].

Grants to historically Black colleges and universities, tribal colleges, and other minority-serving institutions would cover unmet need for enrolled students, with 95 percent of funds disbursed by financial need [S2][S3].
Dreamer students who entered the US before age 16 and meet education criteria would become eligible for federal student aid, including Pell Grants [S2][S3].
Each participating state must use 4 percent of grant funds for college completion programs — advisors, tutoring, and microgrants — aimed at raising graduation rates for low-income students [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through a new appropriation of $84 billion in the first year plus open-ended sums through 2031, and state taxpayers, since participating states must maintain their higher education funding at recent levels as a condition of the grant.

drawbacks.text: The program is expensive: it authorizes $84 billion for fiscal 2021 and 'such sums as may be necessary' for the following decade, a permanent new federal entitlement on top of existing aid [S3].

The tuition cap freezes prices at their 2021 levels rather than rolling them back, so existing high tuition becomes the baseline, and states get a 5-year deadline with waivers available, meaning the debt-free promise could arrive late or in partial form [S3].

States only join voluntarily; a state that opts out or later withdraws leaves its students without coverage, and the enforcement mechanism (probation and withholding funds) depends on federal oversight holding up [S3].
Making Dreamer students eligible for federal financial aid was certain to draw Republican opposition, narrowing the bill's path in a 50-50 Senate [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For students now taking on loans to attend public colleges, the benefit is direct and large: unmet need covered, tuition capped, and completion support added. The cost is a major new federal spending commitment whose size depends on how many states join, and the design hedges against states gaming the program with maintenance-of-effort rules and oversight. The main design weakness is that tuition caps lock in current prices rather than lowering them, and coverage depends entirely on voluntary state participation.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee in April 2021, and the committee never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Brian Schatz introduced the bill on April 21, 2021, joined by eight Democratic cosponsors including Sens. Gillibrand, Booker, Brown, Durbin, and Warren [S1][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, where it stayed for the remainder of the Congress [S5].
No further action — no committee hearing, no markup, no floor vote — appears in the full action history [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No committee or floor vote ever happened, so colleges' tuition levels and students' loan burdens stayed as they were; the federal student loan system and state budget statuses quo both remained untouched.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo: lenders and colleges' pricing stayed intact

for.name: Sen. Brian Schatz
for.role: U.S. Senator from Hawaii, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Debt-Free College Act of 2021 in the Senate on April 21, 2021.

for.name: 8 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Gillibrand, Merkley, Booker, Brown, Baldwin, Blumenthal, Durbin, and Warren).

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in April 2021 and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 9 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, in a Senate with 50 Republicans, 48 Democrats, and 2 Independents.

industries.industry: Federal and private student loan lenders
industries.note: If students' unmet need at public colleges is covered by grants, far less borrowing is needed, shrinking the market for student loans. The bill's passage would have directly reduced loan volume.

States receive grants equal to their net operating support, plus funding for capacity and completion programs, in exchange for tuition caps and maintenance-of-effort requirements. Public higher education gains both money and protected demand.

industries.industry: Historically Black colleges, tribal colleges, and minority-serving institutions
industries.note: A new $3 billion grant program would fund them to cover enrolled students' unmet need, with 95 percent going directly to student aid — a major revenue source, though conditional on capping tuition and maintaining enrollment of low-income students.
The bill routes aid only to public institutions and excludes recently converted for-profit colleges from the minority-serving grant program, cutting them out of the new funding entirely.
